title: Building anatomical terms from word parts
blurb: Decode anatomical names from their position prefixes and structure roots, so you can place a structure such as the pericardium or an intercostal muscle without memorizing it.
question: An imaging report mentions a suprarenal mass, swelling over an intercostal space and an intact periosteum. Where is each structure, and which word parts tell you?

teach.h: An anatomical name is a map label
teach.body: Formally, most anatomical terms combine a prefix that gives a position, a root (combining form) that names a structure, and a suffix such as -al, -ic or -ous meaning 'pertaining to.' In plain English: where it is plus what it is next to. Pericardium = peri- (around) + cardi (heart): the sac around the heart. Subcutaneous = sub- (beneath) + cutane (skin): beneath the skin.

teach.caption: Prefix first gives the position, the root gives the landmark: the intercostal muscles fill the spaces between the ribs.

teach.h: The heart wall, named by its parts
teach.caption: The pericardium (peri- = around) is the sac that surrounds all three layers.

teach.h: One letter can move a structure
teach.body: Look-alike parts are where exam options come from. inter- (between) and intra- (within) differ by one letter, and sub- (below) and supra- (above) are opposites that both start with s. nephr/o (kidney) looks like neur/o (nerve), and oste/o (bone) sits beside chondr/o (cartilage). Read every part of an option: an answer can have the right root with the wrong prefix, or the right prefix with the wrong root.

teach.caption: Osteoblasts build bone matrix, osteoclasts break it down, and osteocytes are mature bone cells.
Hypochondriac regions lie below the rib cartilages on each side of the top row; epigastric is the middle of the top row, hypogastric the middle of the bottom row.

teach.h: Scenario: Jordan reads an imaging report
teach.body: Jordan, applying to a radiography program, shadows a technologist and reads: 'suprarenal mass ruled out; swelling over the left intercostal space; periosteum of the rib intact.' Prefix first: supra- (above) + ren (kidney) puts the first structure on top of the kidney, the adrenal gland. inter- (between) + cost (rib) is the gap between ribs. peri- (around) + oste (bone) is the membrane around the rib.

teach.text: inter- means BETWEEN (intercostal muscles lie between ribs); intra- means WITHIN (intracranial means inside the skull). The hypochondriac region is below the rib cartilage, not a worried patient. nephr/o is kidney, neur/o is nerve. Abduction moves a limb AWAY from the midline; adduction brings it toward.

items: Prefix = position, root = structure, suffix -al/-ic/-ous = pertaining to.
epi- upon, peri- around, endo-/intra- within, inter- between.
sub-/hypo- below, supra- above, ab- away from, ad- toward.
cardi heart, nephr/ren kidney, hepat liver, oste bone, chondr cartilage, cost rib, crani skull.
-blast builds, -clast breaks down, -cyte is a cell.

summary: You can now decode anatomical names by splitting them into position prefixes (epi-, peri-, endo-, sub-, supra-, inter-, intra-, hypo-) and structure roots (cardi/o, nephr/o, oste/o, chondr/o, crani/o, cost/o). You can also spot the look-alike parts that HESI A2 options use as traps.

A.q: Based on its word parts, the endocardium is the layer of the heart that
options: lines the inside of the chambers
covers the outer surface of the heart
forms the thick muscular middle wall
surrounds the heart as a loose sac
A.why: endo- means within and cardi means heart, so the endocardium is the inner lining of the chambers (and it covers the valves).

whyNot.1: The outer surface is the epicardium (epi- = upon).
whyNot.2: The muscular middle layer is the myocardium (my/o = muscle).
whyNot.3: The sac around the heart is the pericardium (peri- = around).

A.why: inter- means between, as in intercostal (between the ribs) and intervertebral (between the vertebrae).

whyNot.0: intra- means within, as in intracranial (inside the skull).
whyNot.2: infra- means below, as in infraorbital (below the eye socket).
whyNot.3: peri- means around, as in pericardium.

A.q: The combining form chondr/o refers to which tissue?
A.why: chondr/o means cartilage, as in chondrocyte (cartilage cell) and the hypochondriac regions (below the rib cartilages).

whyNot.0: Bone is oste/o, as in osteocyte.
whyNot.1: Muscle is my/o, as in myocardium.
whyNot.3: Nerve is neur/o, as in neuron.

B.q: Based on its word parts, intracellular fluid is found
B.why: intra- means within and cellul means cell, so intracellular fluid is the fluid inside cells.

whyNot.0: Fluid between cells would be intercellular (inter- = between), the look-alike term.

B.q: Based on its word parts, a subcutaneous injection is placed
B.why: sub- means beneath and cutane means skin, so a subcutaneous injection goes into the tissue beneath the skin.

whyNot.0: Within the skin would be intradermal (intra- = within).
whyNot.2: Into a muscle is intramuscular (my/o, muscul = muscle).
whyNot.3: Into a vein is intravenous (ven/o = vein).

B.q: Which term names the muscle layer of the heart wall?
B.why: my/o means muscle and cardi means heart, so the myocardium is the heart's cardiac muscle layer.

whyNot.0: peri- means around: the pericardium is the sac around the heart.
whyNot.1: epi- means upon: the epicardium covers the outer surface.
whyNot.3: endo- means within: the endocardium lines the chambers.

C.q: The epigastric and hypogastric regions both lie on the midline. Based on their prefixes, how are they placed?
options: Epigastric above the stomach; hypogastric below it
Epigastric below the stomach; hypogastric above it
Both lie above the stomach, on either side of it
Both lie below the rib cartilages on each side
C.why: epi- means upon (above) and hypo- means below, with gastr meaning stomach. The epigastric region is the top-middle region; the hypogastric region is the bottom-middle region.

whyNot.1: This reverses the prefixes: epi- is upon or above, hypo- is below.
whyNot.2: Only the epigastric region lies above the stomach; the regions on either side of it are the hypochondriac regions.
whyNot.3: Below the rib cartilages describes the hypochondriac regions (chondr = cartilage), not the gastric ones.

C.q: During an exam, a patient has weakness when moving the left arm toward the body's midline. Which movement is weak?
C.why: ad- means toward, so adduction moves a limb toward the midline.

whyNot.0: ab- means away from: abduction moves the arm away from the midline.
whyNot.2: Rotation turns a limb around its long axis.
whyNot.3: Extension straightens a joint or moves the limb backward.

C.q: Based on its root, the hepatic portal vein carries blood to which organ?
C.why: hepat/o means liver: the hepatic portal vein carries blood from the stomach and intestines to the liver.

whyNot.0: The kidney is nephr/o or ren/o (renal vein).
whyNot.1: The stomach is gastr/o (gastric vein); it drains into the hepatic portal vein.
whyNot.2: The heart is cardi/o; blood reaches it later through the inferior vena cava.

reteach.title: Read it like a street address
reteach.question: A street address says where something is relative to a landmark. How does an anatomical name do the same job?

blocks.body: 'Between 5th and 6th Street' or 'above the bakery' tells you where to go from a landmark. An anatomical name works the same way. The prefix is the direction word (between, above, around, within) and the root is the landmark (rib, kidney, heart, skull). Intercostal: between the ribs. Suprarenal: above the kidney. Intracranial: inside the skull.

blocks.text: Change one letter and the address moves: an intercostal space is between ribs, but intracostal would mean inside a rib.

explain.body: epi- upon, peri- around, endo- and intra- within, inter- between, sub- and hypo- below, supra- above, ab- away from, ad- toward.

test.q: Based on its prefix, an intervertebral disc lies
test.why: inter- means between, so intervertebral discs sit between adjacent vertebrae.

whyNot.0: Inside a vertebra would use intra-.

explain.body: The root names the landmark: cardi heart, pulmon/pneum lung, hepat liver, nephr/ren kidney, gastr stomach, enter intestine, oste bone, chondr cartilage, my muscle, neur nerve, derm/cutane skin, crani skull, cost rib.

test.q: Which pair of roots both refer to the kidney?
test.why: nephr/o (Greek) and ren/o (Latin) both mean kidney, as in nephron and renal artery.

whyNot.1: ren/o is kidney, but neur/o means nerve, the look-alike of nephr/o.
whyNot.2: nephr/o is kidney, but hepat/o means liver.
whyNot.3: pulmon/o and pneum/o both refer to the lung.

explain.body: The heart wall shows how prefixes place layers: epicardium (upon) on the outside, myocardium (muscle) in the middle, endocardium (within) lining the chambers, and the pericardium (around) as the surrounding sac.

test.q: Which layer of the heart is named for lying upon its outer surface?
test.why: epi- means upon, so the epicardium lies on the outer surface of the heart wall.

whyNot.0: endo- means within: the endocardium lines the chambers.
whyNot.2: my/o means muscle: the myocardium is the middle muscle layer.
whyNot.3: peri- means around: the pericardium is the sac around the heart, not a layer of its wall.

explain.body: -blast means builder, -clast means breaker and -cyte means cell. Osteoblasts build bone, osteoclasts break it down, osteocytes are mature bone cells, and chondrocytes are cartilage cells.

test.q: Based on its word parts, a chondrocyte is
options: a cell that breaks down cartilage
test.why: chondr/o means cartilage and -cyte means cell, so a chondrocyte is a cartilage cell.

whyNot.0: A bone-building cell is an osteoblast (oste/o + -blast).
whyNot.1: -clast means breaker, but the term here ends in -cyte, a cell.
whyNot.3: Muscle is my/o; chondr/o means cartilage.
